Below is a synthesis of what “motor imaginary” can mean across psychology, neuroscience, motor control, and robotics, with definitions, mechanisms, and applications, and pointers to where “imaginary” is literal (math) versus figurative (simulated/virtual).

What “motor imaginary” refers to
- In cognitive neuroscience and psychology, motor imagery (MI) is commonly defined as a “mental simulation” or “mental rehearsal” of movements without overt motor output, strongly grounded in the body and sharing control mechanisms with actual movement planning and preparation <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery is a cognitive ability commonly defined as ‘mental simulation' or ‘mental rehearsal' of movements without actual movements… it appears to share the control mechanisms and neural substrates with actual movement</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery relates to motor planning and motor preparation, possibly involving ‘suppressed' motor execution; neural mechanisms depend on which stage is engaged</cite>. MI can be organized by perspective (first-person vs third-person) and sensory emphasis (kinesthetic vs visual), and it is distinct from “mental practice” (the training protocol that leverages MI) <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery… does not necessarily represent a homogenous capability… related to planning/preparation and associated with virtual perceptions of visual, auditory, somatosensory and vestibular sensations</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-1">There are two types of motor imagery: in first-person and in third-person… motor imagery should be distinguished from mental practice, the second refers to the process of mental training that takes advantage of the first process</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-2">Annett… internal (kinesthetic) vs external (visual) perspectives; kinesthetic imagery activates cortical motor areas better than visual imagery</cite>.

Mechanisms: shared motor control and neural signatures
- Convergent neuroimaging and TMS evidence shows MI activates motor and premotor cortices in patterns similar to movement execution, with corticospinal excitability modulations and muscle-specific motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) during imagery of targeted actions <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Strong supporting evidence… TMS studies showing motor imagery enhanced corticospinal excitability</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-2">During motor imagery… there is an increase in MEP amplitude compared to at rest, with increases in the muscles involved in imagined movements; kinesthetic imagery activates the cortical motor better than visual imagery</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-4">An activation pattern similar to that of execution of an actual action… increase in gamma-band power during imaginary movement with spatial overlap to actual movement</cite>. Broader networks including cerebellum, basal ganglia, SMA, PMC, and parietal cortices are recruited, consistent with planning and preparation overlapping with execution but blocked at the corticospinal level <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery… shares control mechanisms and neural substrates with actual movement</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-4">The motor imagery belongs to the programming/preparation of actual actions, with differences being that execution is blocked at the corticospinal level</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-2">The observation of other individuals performing skilled movements, as well as MI, was effective for motor training; M1, premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, and parietal cortices are activated</cite>.

- Perspective and agency modulate motor resonance and corticospinal excitability. First-person MI/observation with a sense of control engages stronger motor resonance (mirroring-like activity) and attenuates certain visual-illusion effects, whereas third-person observation shows weaker resonance and less illusion-of-control; intention to imitate can increase facilitation during observation, and combined observation+imagery (“dual-simulation”) further boosts excitability beyond either alone <cite id="cb7e6a46-0">Biological motion modulates the flash-lag effect; first-person perspective with tracking diminishes the illusion (attenuation consistent with an illusion of control), whereas third-person tracking shows no illusion due to weaker motor resonance</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-0">Observing a movement with the intention to imitate elicits greater corticospinal facilitation than passive observation; previous work shows observation with intent-to-imitate facilitates M1 excitability</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-2">Combined observation and imagery facilitates corticospinal excitability more than passive observation; convergent TMS/fMRI evidence shows greater motor activity when observation and imagery are combined</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-3">Traditional imagery activates premotor cortex and other motor regions similarly to observation (though less strongly); combining processes can yield stronger resonance</cite>.

- Electrophysiological biomarkers link MI to motor system state. In healthy participants, event-related desynchronization (ERD) in sensorimotor bands during MI tracks M1 excitability: larger ERD correlates with larger MEPs and reduced intracortical inhibition, and can serve as a state-dependent trigger for BMI paradigms that selectively disinhibit agonist output; ERD magnitude also associates with increased spinal motoneuron excitability (F-wave persistence) <cite id="7f1734df-4">ERD during motor imagery of wrist movement was associated with increased MEP amplitudes and reduced SICI; ERD magnitude represented M1 excitability</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">ERD magnitude during hand motor imagery associated with increased F-wave persistence, suggesting increased excitability at cortical and spinal levels</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">Motor imagery-based BMI can selectively disinhibit corticomotor output to the agonist muscle using brain state–dependent TMS</cite>.

Dynamical and “virtual” perspectives on the “imaginary” motor
- Motor control can be modeled with body models and “virtual” force fields: the Passive Motion Paradigm treats the body as a spring-like network in a potential field; active control updates inputs to cancel “virtual” perturbations toward a target, yielding attractor dynamics that recapitulate synergies in a true motor format. This connects to the Mental Simulation account in which the brain simulates executed actions internally so the motor system reads the “imagined” plan as a real action <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">Mental Simulation Theory posits the brain generates a simulation-state flow that produces a true motor format so that it would be regarded by the motor system as a real action</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">PMP… an internal body model of spring-like elements with a global potential energy; an attractor neurodynamics toward equilibrium states</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">Relationship between PMP and Active Inference: anti-symmetry between active inference and passive motion reflects complementary views of using forward models to generate predictions of sensed movements</cite>.

- Biological motion and symbolic dynamics obey kinematic constraints (e.g., the 1/3 power law), and reproducing such dynamics is shaped by perception–action coupling. Visual and auditory motion dynamics bias drawn/replicated trajectories; incongruent kinematics distort reproduced geometry in feedforward ways, underscoring how motor output is guided by internalized dynamics the system treats as “virtual” constraints <cite id="cb7e6a46-1">Biological motion is characterized by the 1/3 power law vt = KC^(-1/3); human tracking is facilitated when motion complies with the law</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-4">Circular visual motions can be distorted by sounds; visuo–motor coupling with incongruent elliptical kinematics led to elliptical reproduction; motor reproduction is constrained by co-variations between curvature and kinematic properties in a feedforward manner</cite>. Multisensory entrainment to complex rhythms (e.g., Lorenz-like attractors) may require coordinating posture to nonlocal temporal structures, anticipating future states rather than just local time-scale prediction, suggesting that “imaginary” attractor dynamics guide sensorimotor tracking even without overt movement <cite id="cb7e6a46-2">Entraining to a Lorenz attractor derived signal requires coordination of posture to the global temporal structure; anticipatory control depends on past, current, and future states; complex stimulus motion demands continuous pursuit, explaining stronger gaze–target coupling</cite>.

Perception–action links: imagery, observation, and congruence
- MI, movement observation, and mirror neuron activity share circuits but differ in strength and timing; dual-simulation (simultaneous imagery while observing) yields stronger motor facilitation than either alone. Corticospinal excitability changes during combined observation+imagery exceed those during observation or imagery in isolation, and EMG activity differences are not confounding in these paradigms <cite id="7f1734df-2">Combined observation and imagery facilitated corticospinal excitability more than passive observation; increased facilitation was not due to higher EMG; differences in coil position were non-significant</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-3">Observation and imagery activate similar brain areas but with different magnitudes/timing; combining processes may cause stronger resonance and increased corticospinal excitability</cite>. First-person perspective typically elicits stronger motor resonance and weaker illusion-of-control effects than third-person, consistent with stronger engagement of efference copies and body-schema alignment during imagined/observed self-agency <cite id="cb7e6a46-0">First-person tracking attenuates the flash-lag illusion consistent with an illusion of control; third-person tracking shows no illusion due to generally weaker motor resonance</cite>.

- Imagery specificity and modality matter for training. Kinesthetic-first-person imagery tends to optimize performance more than visual-only, and MI can enhance skill acquisition and sequence learning; MI also supports neurorehabilitation and BMI control by recruiting motor networks without movement, enabling effector-specific up-training in healthy and patient populations <cite id="a650a1a8-1">The most effective for learning is that first-person; numerous studies show performance is optimized through motor imagery</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-2">Kinesthetic imagery activates the cortical motor better than visual imagery</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery… offers an essential basis for the development of brain–machine/brain–computer interfaces for physically disabled persons</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-1">MI plays a critical role in motor skill learning and sports training, as well as prosthesis control and motor rehabilitation</cite>.

Practical frameworks and assessment
- Taxonomy and training prescriptions:
  - Perspective: first-person (internal/kinesthetic) vs third-person (external/visual) <cite id="a650a1a8-1">First-person vs third-person imagery definitions; first-person often most effective</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-2">Internal (kinesthetic) vs external (visual) perspectives; kinesthetic activates motor cortex more</cite>.
  - Sensory channels: emphasize kinesthetic/proprioceptive imagery to boost corticospinal engagement; integrate observation to leverage mirror mechanisms and increase excitability beyond imagery alone <cite id="7f1734df-2">Combined observation+imagery yields greater corticospinal excitability than either alone</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-3">Observation activates motor regions with less magnitude than imagery; combining processes increases resonance</cite>.
  - Agency/intent: instruct to imagine oneself performing (or controlling) the action to strengthen motor resonance and reduce dissociation effects (e.g., flash-lag attenuation) <cite id="cb7e6a46-0">Illusion of control counteracts the flash-lag effect; emerges with first-person tracking/agency</cite>.

- Neurophysiological monitoring:
  - TMS/MEP: muscle-specific MEP increases during MI confirm recruitment of agonists; SICI reductions and increased ERD track rising corticospinal excitability and can gate BMI-enabled output <cite id="a650a1a8-2">MEP amplitude increases only in muscles involved in imagined movements</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">ERD magnitude represents M1 excitability; associated with increased MEPs and reduced SICI; used for state-dependent TMS to selectively disinhibit agonists</cite>.
  - EEG/MEG: gamma-band event-related synchronization/desynchronization overlaps with execution, supporting shared motor planning signatures in MI <cite id="a650a1a8-4">During imaginary movement of the hand, there is an increase in gamma-band power with significant spatial overlap to actual movement</cite>.

- Rehabilitation and assistive use:
  - MI-based neurorehabilitation can harness motor network plasticity when overt movement is impaired; BMI/BCI paradigms can use MI-driven ERD states to selectively uptrain agonists and restore effective output in paralysis models <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery… offers an essential basis for the development of BMIs/BCIs for physically disabled persons</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">Motor imagery-based BMI selectively disinhibits corticomotor output to the agonist muscle; ERD magnitude links to increased excitability at cortical and spinal levels</cite>.

When “imaginary” is literal vs figurative
- Imaginary numbers/complex quaternions: While contemporary motor control typically uses real-valued kinematics with occasional complex-valued signal analyses (e.g., Fourier/EEG), the core “imaginary motor” concept is more about internal simulation (MI) or virtual dynamics (force fields, attractors) rather than complex algebra per se. Still, complex-valued methods (e.g., transforms) are often used to analyze motor-related rhythms and ERD/ERS, and attractor models (Lorenz-like) describe internal state dynamics that guide posture and gaze tracking even without overt movement <cite id="cb7e6a46-2">Entraining to Lorenz attractor motion requires coordinating posture to global temporal structure; complex stimulus motion demands anticipatory gaze control</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-4">Imaginary movement increases gamma-band power with spatial overlap to actual movement, indicating shared planning signatures</cite>. In robotics and computational neuroscience, “virtual” force fields and body models formalize how imagined goals induce real-like internal dynamics to produce motor plans <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">PMP… virtual perturbations to a designated target drive active synergy formation via body-model dynamics; relationship to active inference</cite>.

Putting it together: how to use “motor imaginary” in practice
- If your goal is skill learning or performance enhancement, train first-person, kinesthetic-rich imagery; integrate observation of the target action to exploit mirror mechanisms; and structure tasks to induce agency/control to strengthen motor resonance and reduce perceptual dissociations <cite id="a650a1a8-1">First-person imagery is most effective for learning; performance is optimized through motor imagery</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-2">Combined observation+imagery yields greater corticospinal excitability than passive observation</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-0">Illusion of control in first-person conditions attenuates the flash-lag effect, consistent with stronger motor resonance</cite>. 
- If your goal is neurorehabilitation or assistive control, leverage MI to recruit motor networks even without movement, monitor MEP/ERD/SICI to quantify engagement, and use state-dependent TMS/BCI to selectively disinhibit agonists for effector-specific uptraining <cite id="a650a1a8-0">MI shares mechanisms with actual movement and underlies BMI/BCI development</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">ERD magnitude during MI reflects corticospinal excitability and can gate selective motor output in BMI paradigms</cite>.
- If modeling or interpreting “imaginary” movement dynamics, consider body-model/force-field attractors and kinematic constraints (e.g., 1/3 power law) as the “virtual” scaffolds that shape both imagined and executed behavior across modalities <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">Body-model attractor dynamics with virtual force fields implement motor plans</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-1">Biological motion follows the 1/3 power law; compliance facilitates tracking</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-4">Auditory and visual dynamics bias reproduced motion geometry; motor reproduction is constrained by curvature–kinematic covariations</cite>.

Open questions and cautions
- Imagery quality varies across individuals; visual experience and intent-to-imitate modulate excitability in nuanced ways, and group differences (e.g., visual experience) may not always correlate directly with MEP changes, underscoring heterogeneous mechanisms and the importance of personalized protocols <cite id="7f1734df-0">Visual experience did not affect corticospinal excitability during observation; there is a correlation between MEP changes during imagery and imagery ability, though imagery ability groups showed no group × condition interaction</cite>. 
- Perspective and sensory dominance interact with agency; third-person observation and visual-only imagery recruit motor networks but with weaker excitability and motor resonance than first-person/kinesthetic imagery, suggesting that “how” one imagines matters as much as “whether” one imagines <cite id="a650a1a8-2">Kinesthetic imagery activates cortical motor better than visual</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-3">Observation and imagery produce similar but not identical motor activations; combining them increases facilitation</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-0">Third-person perspective generally shows weaker motor resonance and no illusion of control</cite>. 
- The phrase “imaginary motor” can be ambiguous; in most contemporary motor science it denotes MI or virtual/internal dynamics rather than literal complex arithmetic. Where precision is required, specify “motor imagery,” “virtual force fields/body models,” or “attractor dynamics” to avoid confusion. Where complex numbers are used, they typically appear as analytic tools (signals/spectra) or kinematic constraints, not as direct motor commands <cite id="a650a1a8-4">Imaginary movement shares gamma-band activation patterns with execution</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-2">Lorenz attractor tracking engages anticipatory, nonlocal coordination in posture and gaze</cite>.

In short: “Motor imaginary” spans (1) the cognitive act of motor imagery—an embodied rehearsal that recruits motor-planning circuits with muscle-specific excitability; (2) dynamical models in which the brain and robot simulate “virtual” force fields and attractors that guide action without movement; and (3) multisensory, agency-linked processes where first-person, kinesthetic-rich simulation and combined observation produce the strongest motor facilitation and learning. These perspectives converge on the idea that imagined movement is not merely “in the head,” but engages motor systems in ways that can be measured, trained, and harnessed for performance and rehabilitation <cite id="a650a1a8-0">Motor imagery is a mental simulation that shares mechanisms and neural substrates with actual movement</cite> <cite id="a650a1a8-4">Imagined movement elicits gamma-band increases and motor network activation patterns similar to execution</cite> <cite id="cb7e6a46-3">Body-model/virtual-force paradigms implement motor plans as attractor dynamics read by motor systems</cite> <cite id="7f1734df-4">ERD-linked state-dependent TMS during motor imagery can selectively uptrain agonist output for BMI-based neurorehabilitation</cite>.

Title: Organizing motor imageries.
Snippet: Motor imagery, or motor imagination, has been a popular topic of research in, but not limited to, psychology, cognitive neuroscience, neurophysiology, neuroimaging and clinical neurology. One reason for such disseminated interest stems from a unique property of motor imagery as a cognitive ability strongly grounded to the body, or 'embodied' cognition. An archetypal example is motor imagery used implicitly for visual shape discrimination (Parsons et al., 1995). Moreover, motor imagery, albeit a cognitive entity, appears to share the control mechanisms and neural substrates with actual movement, providing a unique opportunity to study neural control of movement. Strong supporting evidence for this statement is available from many transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies showing motor imagery enhanced corticospinal excitability (Izumi et al., 1995;Kasai et al., 1997;Liang et al., 2007;Mizuguchi et al., 2013;Stinear and Byblow, 2003). Motor imagery also draws attention as a technique for sports training and neuro-rehabilitation. More recently, motor imagery offers an essential basis for the development of brain-machine/brain-computer interfaces (BMIs/BCIs) for physically disabled persons. 

Motor imagery is a cognitive ability commonly defined as 'mental simulation' or 'mental rehearsal' of movements without actual movements (Decety, 1996;Grush, 2004;Jeannerod, 1994). This definition has been widely accepted in the field, and reasonably encompasses a variety of motor imagery studies conducted so far. However, it should be noted that motor imagery, as it currently stands, does not necessarily represent a homogenous capability. From the perspective of motor control, motor imagery relates to motor planning and motor preparation, which are possibly related to 'suppressed' motor execution. Neural mechanisms should be different, depending on which stage of motor control is mainly involved in a particular motor imagery task or in an individual's strategy. Similarly, motor imagery can be divergent, depending upon the extent to which a task or a strategy is associated with virtual perception of visual, auditory, somatosensory (kinesthetic), and vestibular sensations, all of which can be associated with overt actions.
</snippet>

Title: Seeing Circles and Drawing Ellipses: When Sound Biases Reproduction of Visual Motion
Snippet: It is now well established that biological motion is characterized by specific kinematic properties, for instance, by the 1/3 power law which postulates that the tangential velocity of the motion v t is constrained by the local curvature C of its geometrical trajectory: v t = KC -1/3 with K a constant [1]. Regarding the visual modality, it has been shown that the human ability to track a visual motion with the non-hidden hand is facilitated when the motion complies with the 1/3 power law [2]. Title: Brain-machine Interface (BMI)-based Neurorehabilitation for Post-stroke Upper Limb Paralysis.
Snippet: To clarify the neurophysiological basis of BMI-based neurorehabilitation, Takemi et al. 61 studied the relationship of ERD with primary motor cortex (M1) excitability during motor imagery of right wrist movement as assessed using MEPs, short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) with TMS. Twenty healthy participants performed 7 s of rest followed by 5 s of motor imagery and received online visual feedback of the ERD magnitude of the contralateral hand M1 while performing the motor imagery task. TMS was applied to the right hand M1 when ERD exceeded predetermined thresholds during motor imagery, and MEP amplitudes, SICI, and ICF were recorded from the agonist muscle of the imagined hand movement. It was observed that the large ERD during wrist motor imagery was associated with significantly increased MEP amplitudes and reduced SICI but no significant changes in ICF; these findings indicated that the ERD magnitude during wrist motor imagery represents M1 excitability. This study provided electrophysiological evidence that a motor imagery task involving ERD may induce changes in corticospinal excitability similar to changes accompanying actual movements. Takemi et al. 62 further examined the association of ERD during motor imagery with the excitability of spinal motoneurons in 15 healthy participants. The results indicated that the ERD magnitude during hand motor imagery was associated with an increase in F-wave persistence but not with the response average of F-wave amplitude or F-wave latency. These findings suggest that the ERD magnitude may be a biomarker representing increases in the excitability at both cortical and spinal levels. Using brain state-dependent TMS, Takemi et al. 63 also showed that motor imagery-based BMI can selectively disinhibit the corticomotor output to the agonist muscle, enabling effector-specific training in patients with motor paralysis.

An archetypal example is motor imagery used implicitly for visual shape discrimination (Parsons et al., 1995). Moreover, motor imagery, albeit a cognitive entity, appears to share the control mechanisms and neural substrates with actual movement, providing a unique opportunity to study neural control of movement. Strong supporting evidence for this statement is available from many transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies showing motor imagery enhanced corticospinal excitability (Izumi et al., 1995;Kasai et al., 1997;Liang et al., 2007;Mizuguchi et al., 2013;Stinear and Byblow, 2003). Motor imagery also draws attention as a technique for sports training and neuro-rehabilitation. More recently, motor imagery offers an essential basis for the development of brain-machine/brain-computer interfaces (BMIs/BCIs) for physically disabled persons. 

Motor imagery is a cognitive ability commonly defined as 'mental simulation' or 'mental rehearsal' of movements without actual movements (Decety, 1996;Grush, 2004;Jeannerod, 1994). However, it should be noted that motor imagery, as it currently stands, does not necessarily represent a homogenous capability. From the perspective of motor control, motor imagery relates to motor planning and motor preparation, which are possibly related to 'suppressed' motor execution. Neural mechanisms should be different, depending on which stage of motor control is mainly involved in a particular motor imagery task or in an individual's strategy. Similarly, motor imagery can be divergent, depending upon the extent to which a task or a strategy is associated with virtual perception of visual, auditory, somatosensory (kinesthetic), and vestibular sensations, all of which can be associated with overt actions.

Snippet: To clarify the neurophysiological basis of BMI-based neurorehabilitation, Takemi et al. 61 studied the relationship of ERD with primary motor cortex (M1) excitability during motor imagery of right wrist movement as assessed using MEPs, short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) with TMS. TMS was applied to the right hand M1 when ERD exceeded predetermined thresholds during motor imagery, and MEP amplitudes, SICI, and ICF were recorded from the agonist muscle of the imagined hand movement. It was observed that the large ERD during wrist motor imagery was associated with significantly increased MEP amplitudes and reduced SICI but no significant changes in ICF; these findings indicated that the ERD magnitude during wrist motor imagery represents M1 excitability. This study provided electrophysiological evidence that a motor imagery task involving ERD may induce changes in corticospinal excitability similar to changes accompanying actual movements. Takemi et al. 62 further examined the association of ERD during motor imagery with the excitability of spinal motoneurons in 15 healthy participants. The results indicated that the ERD magnitude during hand motor imagery was associated with an increase in F-wave persistence but not with the response average of F-wave amplitude or F-wave latency. These findings suggest that the ERD magnitude may be a biomarker representing increases in the excitability at both cortical and spinal levels. Using brain state-dependent TMS, Takemi et al. 63 also showed that motor imagery-based BMI can selectively disinhibit the corticomotor output to the agonist muscle, enabling effector-specific training in patients with motor paralysis.

Summary
- Motor imagery training (MIT) does not consistently improve motor outcomes across patient populations and task contexts. Failures or minimal gains are common in populations with severe/chronic deficits, limited sensorimotor feedback, cognitive-linguistic impairments, or when MIT is delivered without tight coupling to physical practice or in settings where imagery vividness and quality cannot be ensured. <cite id="f7762f42-2">Despite early case reports and add-on trials, a larger randomized controlled trial failed to find therapeutic benefit of mental practice in subacute stroke, underscoring that patient selection, training factors, and integration with physiotherapy critically determine outcomes. <cite id="f7762f42-3">Moreover, patients may improve on tasks they rehearsed mentally without gains in broader motor function, indicating limited generalization when foundational impairments remain.</cite>

Patient populations where MIT often fails to improve motor outcomes
- Chronic or severe hemiparesis after stroke: <cite id="f0acdf57-0">In chronic stroke patients, four weeks of unsupervised daily motor imagery of affected-arm movements improved performance on the trained task more than visual imagery controls but showed no transfer to other tasks like pegboard or dynamometer, and did not change perceived control; improvements generalized only to the trained task.</cite> <cite id="f7762f42-2">A larger RCT in patients within six months of stroke found no superiority of motor imagery over visual imagery or standard care, with all groups improving similarly, raising concerns about added value in moderate-to-severe impairment.</cite> <cite id="da2a47b7-1">Meta-analytic summaries suggest that if only high-quality studies are analyzed, overall gains from MIT may disappear, implying that many small, heterogeneous trials overestimate benefits in severe deficits.</cite>
- Spinal cord injury (SCI) with intact peripheral feedback: <cite id="da2a47b7-1">Because intact afferent pathways in incomplete SCI permit conventional practice, MI may add little when patients can perform some movement or receive sensory feedback; several studies report inconsistent efficiency of MI training and emphasize that early, effective motor rehabilitation can dramatically improve outcomes in incomplete SCI, making MI less necessary absent specific deficits.</cite>
- Parkinson disease (PD): <cite id="10d6c7ee-0">Short-term motor imagery practice has repeatedly failed to produce significant motor facilitation in PD cohorts, while longer-term, more structured programs (e.g., kinesthetic imagery with feedback) report improvements in slowness and brain activation; this pattern suggests that brief, unstructured MI often fails to change motor performance.</cite>
- Aphasia and severe communication/attentional limitations: <cite id="f0acdf57-4">In a single-session BCI/FES exoskeleton study, one participant with expressive aphasia (15/30 on Frenchay Aphasia Assessment) could not complete cognitive screening yet still exhibited adequate motor imagery scores; although this is not a longitudinal efficacy study, it illustrates that individuals with expressive aphasia may still retain imagery capacity, but the practical delivery and fidelity of MI-based home programs can be constrained by communication and attentional demands, potentially limiting benefit when these domains are impaired.</cite>

- Unsupervised home-based training without measurable imagery quality: <cite id="f0acdf57-0">When MI was practiced daily at home for four weeks in chronic stroke, gains were limited to the trained task and did not extend to other motor measures; the study also found no effect on perceived control, highlighting that unguided practice and unclear cognitive contributors can blunt transfer.</cite> <cite id="f7762f42-2">The inability to objectively measure imagery performance complicates ensuring adequate dosage and quality, contributing to inconsistent benefits and possible nonresponse.</cite>

- Mitigation strategies: <cite id="f7762f42-2">Use objective imagery assessment (mental chronometry, kinematic constraints) and tailor programs to patient factors; integrate MI as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, physical practice to enhance far transfer.</cite> <cite id="f0acdf57-3">Design task-specific sequences with repeated near-to-far transfer probes (e.g., walking test + Fugl–Meyer) and progressively increase complexity to promote generalized learning rather than mere rehearsal-specific gains.</cite> <cite id="10d6c7ee-0">In PD and other movement disorders, prefer longer-duration programs with feedback (e.g., fMRI-based neurofeedback of insula connectivity) to improve motor planning and timing.</cite> <cite id="da2a47b7-4">In complete SCI, pair MI with functional electrical stimulation or BCI-assisted interfaces to bridge absent efferent pathways and drive central plasticity.</cite>

Evidence gaps and outlook
- Heterogeneity and study quality: <cite id="da2a47b7-1">Meta-analyses indicate that when only high-quality trials are considered, overall gains from MIT become nonsignificant, highlighting publication bias and protocol heterogeneity.</cite> <cite id="f7762f42-2">Future factorial trials that objectively quantify imagery quality, standardize protocols, and pre-register outcomes are needed to delineate nonresponders and moderators like baseline motor severity and sensory status.</cite>

Snippet: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Currently, there is no effective treatment for pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury. Snippet: In a series of studies that have appeared in the last decade (Tamir et al., 2007;Lee et al., 2011;Page et al., 2011;Cho et al., 2012), it was shown that motor imagery training can be beneficial for motor rehabilitation in adult patients with acquired brain damage, in particular stroke (for reviews see Sharma et al., 2006;Dickstein and Deutsch, 2007;Zimmermann-Schlatter et al., 2008;Malouin and Richards, 2010). Motor imagery is supposed to stimulate the neural networks that underlie the planning and control of movements. As such, motor imagery training in rehabilitation is regarded as a 'backdoor' to facilitate a patient's motor performance (Sharma et al., 2006). Despite its proven effectiveness for rehabilitation in adult stroke patients, and despite converging evidence showing that problems in motor imagery are concomitant with motor control problems in congenital motor disorders such as cerebral palsy (CP) and developmental coordination disorder (DCD; Wilson et al., 2001;Crajé et al., 2010), empirical studies on motor imagery training in these children are scarce (but see Wilson et al., 2002). While adults were repeatedly shown to be able to use motor imagery (e.g., Cerritelli et al., 2000;Petit et al., 2003;Choudhury et al., 2007a;ter Horst et al., 2012), children's ability for motor imagery is not very clear. Title: Influence of motor imagery training on gait rehabilitation in sub-acute stroke: A randomized controlled trial.
Snippet: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the effect of mental practice on motor imagery ability and assess the influence of motor imagery on gait rehabilitation in sub-acute stroke.


DESIGN
Randomized controlled trial.


SUBJECTS
A total of 44 patients with gait dysfunction after first-ever stroke were randomly allocated to a motor imagery training group and a muscle relaxation group.


METHODS
The motor imagery group received 6 weeks of daily mental practice. The relaxation group received a muscle relaxation programme of equal duration. Motor imagery ability and lower limb function were assessed at baseline and after 6 weeks of treatment. Motor imagery ability was tested using a questionnaire and mental chronometry test. Gait outcome was evaluated using a 10-m walk test (near transfer) and the Fugl-Meyer assessment (far transfer).


RESULTS
Significant between-group differences were found, with the vividness of kinesthetic imagery and the walking test results improving more in the motor imagery group than in the muscle relaxation group. There was no group interaction effect for the far transfer outcome score.


CONCLUSION
Motor imagery training may have a beneficial task-specific effect on gait function in sub-acute stroke; however, longer term confirmation is required.
</snippet>

Patient populations where MIT often fails to improve motor outcomes

Title: Review of the randomized clinical stroke rehabilitation trials in 2009
Snippet: Mental imagery intervention has been shown to enhance poststroke patients relearning daily task performance [6]. This study assessed the efficacy of mental imagery in promoting generalization of the task skills learned in a training environment to trained and untrained tasks carried out in a novel environment. Thirty-five acute poststroke patients were randomly assigned to the mental imagery (MI; n=18) or conventional functional rehabilitation (FR; n=17) group [7]. The MI intervention was 15 1 hour daily session for 5-days per week for 3 weeks. The standardized practices and daily tasks were broken down into 3 separate activities: chunking-self regulation-mental rehearsal strategies. Thus mental imagery intervention was useful for improving patients' ability to perform the tasks that they were not previously trained on, and in places different from the training environments. The stroke severity (measured by Barthel Index) had no influence on task performance in the MI group while in the FR group if did influence outcome.

Title: Organizing motor imageries.
Snippet: Motor imagery has been a promised neuro-rehabilitation technique (Sharma et al., 2006). This expectation seems rationale, considering the shared neural mechanisms between motor imagery and movement execution. Put simply, an idea behind this is that it may be possible to train the motor representations in the brain through mental practice of movements. A few case series with a small number of stroke patients have provided preliminary evidence for improvement of clinical outcomes and neuroimaging observations (Butler and Page, 2006;Page et al., 2009). Moreover, two randomized controlled trials combining motor imagery practices and conventional physiotherapy showed results pointing toward the add-on effects of motor imagery training (Liu et al., 2009;Page et al., 2007). Despite these promises, a recent randomized controlled trial with a larger cohort than before failed to find the therapeutic benefit of mental practice of movements in patients within 6 months following stroke (Ietswaart et al., 2011). This study included three groups receiving different interventions: motor imagery, visual imagery, and standard care. Although all groups showed improvement of outcome measures, there were no differences in improvement across the three groups. Hence, it remains to be seen if the motor imagery technique really has therapeutic effects in comparison with other types of interventions. There are many issues to be considered for future clinical trials: factors contributing training effects, patient selection, a way to integrate motor imagery with conventional physiotherapy, and so forth (Malouin et al., 2013). Title: Brain Activation Evoked by Motor Imagery in Pediatric Patients with Complete Spinal Cord Injury
Snippet: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Currently, there is no effective treatment for pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury. Motor imagery has been proposed as an alternative to physical training for patients who are unable to move voluntarily. Our aim was to reveal the potential mechanism of motor imagery in the rehabilitation of pediatric complete spinal cord injury. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-six pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury and 26 age- and sex-matched healthy children as healthy controls were recruited. All participants underwent the motor imagery task-related fMRI scans, and additional motor execution scans were performed only on healthy controls. First, we compared the brain-activation patterns between motor imagery and motor execution in healthy controls. Then, we compared the brain activation of motor imagery between the 2 groups and compared the brain activation of motor imagery in pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury and that of motor execution in healthy controls. RESULTS: In healthy controls, compared with motor execution, motor imagery showed increased activation in the left inferior parietal lobule and decreased activation in the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule, middle cingulate cortex, and right insula. In addition, our results revealed that the 2 groups both activated the bilateral supplementary motor area, middle cingulate cortex and left inferior parietal lobule, and supramarginal gyrus during motor imagery. Compared with healthy controls, higher activation in the bilateral paracentral lobule, supplementary motor area, putamen, and cerebellar lobules III–V was detected in pediatric complete spinal cord injury during motor imagery, and the activation of these regions was even higher than that of healthy controls during motor execution. CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrated that part of the motor imagery network was functionally preserved in pediatric complete spinal cord injury and could be activated through motor imagery. In addition, higher-level activation in sensorimotor-related regions was also found in pediatric complete spinal cord injury during motor imagery. Our findings may provide a theoretic basis for the application of motor imagery training in pediatric complete spinal cord injury.

Title: Effects of motor imagery training after chronic, complete spinal cord injury
Snippet: Abnormalities in brain motor system function are present following spinal cord injury (SCI) and could reduce effectiveness of restorative interventions. Motor imagery training, which can improve motor behavior and modulate brain function, might address this concern but has not been examined in subjects with SCI. Ten subjects with SCI and complete tetra-/paraplegia plus ten healthy controls underwent assessment before and after 7 days of motor imagery training to tongue and to foot. Motor imagery training significantly improved the behavioral outcome measure, speed of movement, in non-paralyzed muscles. Training was also associated with increased fMRI activation in left putamen, an area associated with motor learning, during attempted right foot movement in both groups, despite foot movements being present in controls and absent in subjects with SCI. This fMRI change was absent in a second healthy control group serially imaged without training. In subjects with SCI, training exaggerated, rather than normalized, baseline derangement of left globus pallidus activation. The current study found that motor imagery training improves motor performance and alters brain function in subjects with complete SCI despite lack of voluntary motor control and peripheral feedback. These effects of motor imagery training on brain function have not been previously described in a neurologically impaired population, and were similar to those found in healthy controls. Motor imagery might be of value as one component of a restorative intervention.

documents.snippet: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Currently, there is no effective treatment for pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury. Motor imagery has been proposed as an alternative to physical training for patients who are unable to move voluntarily. Our aim was to reveal the potential mechanism of motor imagery in the rehabilitation of pediatric complete spinal cord injury. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-six pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury and 26 age- and sex-matched healthy children as healthy controls were recruited. All participants underwent the motor imagery task-related fMRI scans, and additional motor execution scans were performed only on healthy controls. First, we compared the brain-activation patterns between motor imagery and motor execution in healthy controls. Then, we compared the brain activation of motor imagery between the 2 groups and compared the brain activation of motor imagery in pediatric patients with complete spinal cord injury and that of motor execution in healthy controls. RESULTS: In healthy controls, compared with motor execution, motor imagery showed increased activation in the left inferior parietal lobule and decreased activation in the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule, middle cingulate cortex, and right insula. In addition, our results revealed that the 2 groups both activated the bilateral supplementary motor area, middle cingulate cortex and left inferior parietal lobule, and supramarginal gyrus during motor imagery. Compared with healthy controls, higher activation in the bilateral paracentral lobule, supplementary motor area, putamen, and cerebellar lobules III–V was detected in pediatric complete spinal cord injury during motor imagery, and the activation of these regions was even higher than that of healthy controls during motor execution. CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrated that part of the motor imagery network was functionally preserved in pediatric complete spinal cord injury and could be activated through motor imagery. In addition, higher-level activation in sensorimotor-related regions was also found in pediatric complete spinal cord injury during motor imagery. Our findings may provide a theoretic basis for the application of motor imagery training in pediatric complete spinal cord injury.

Title: The Effectiveness of Visuo- Motor Behavior Rehearsal (VMBR) to Reduce the Anxiety and to Improve Self Concept for Athletes with Special Needs
Snippet: OBJECTIVE: To assess the efficacy of motor imagery training for arm function in chronic stroke patients. The relation between mental processes such as attentional and perceived personal control over recovery, and motor imagery was additionally investigated. DESIGN AND SUBJECTS: Twenty patients with long-term motor impairments (mean two years post stroke), were assessed before and after four weeks of training. Ten patients mentally rehearsed movements with their affected arm. Their recovery was compared with patients who performed non-motor imagery (n =5), or who were not engaged in mental rehearsal (n=5). SETTING: Patients were recruited from the stroke database of Ninewells Hospital, Dundee. Assessment and training were performed at the patients' home. INTERVENTIONS: The motor imagery group was asked to practice daily imagining moving tokens with their affected arm. The non-motor imagery group rehearsed visual imagery of previously seen pictures. All patients practiced physically moving the tokens. MAIN MEASURES: The following variables were assessed before and after training: motor function (training task, pegboard and dynamometer), perceived locus of control, attention control and ADL independence. RESULTS: All patient groups improved on all motor tasks except the dynamometer. Improvement was greater for the motor imagery group on the training task only (average of 14% versus 6%). No effect of motor imagery training was found on perceived or attentional control. CONCLUSIONS: Motor imagery training without supervision at home may improve performance on the trained task only. The relation between movement imagery, attention and perceived personal control over recovery remained unclear(Dijkerman; Ietswaart ; Johnston ; MacWalter, 2004, P.P. 538-549).

Title: Current insights in the development of children’s motor imagery ability
Snippet: In a series of studies that have appeared in the last decade (Tamir et al., 2007;Lee et al., 2011;Page et al., 2011;Cho et al., 2012), it was shown that motor imagery training can be beneficial for motor rehabilitation in adult patients with acquired brain damage, in particular stroke (for reviews see Sharma et al., 2006;Dickstein and Deutsch, 2007;Zimmermann-Schlatter et al., 2008;Malouin and Richards, 2010). Motor imagery is supposed to stimulate the neural networks that underlie the planning and control of movements. As such, motor imagery training in rehabilitation is regarded as a 'backdoor' to facilitate a patient's motor performance (Sharma et al., 2006). Despite its proven effectiveness for rehabilitation in adult stroke patients, and despite converging evidence showing that problems in motor imagery are concomitant with motor control problems in congenital motor disorders such as cerebral palsy (CP) and developmental coordination disorder (DCD; Wilson et al., 2001;Crajé et al., 2010), empirical studies on motor imagery training in these children are scarce (but see Wilson et al., 2002). A likely reason for this lack of research may be that the successful application of motor imagery training necessitates that the individual has a skilled capacity to perform motor imagery. While adults were repeatedly shown to be able to use motor imagery (e.g., Cerritelli et al., 2000;Petit et al., 2003;Choudhury et al., 2007a;ter Horst et al., 2012), children's ability for motor imagery is not very clear. The present study reviews the empirical literature on motor imagery in children to delineate the capacity of children up to 12 years of age to engage in motor imagery. The studies that were selected after a search in the literature are analyzed to provide answers to two research questions. How does motor imagery develop during childhood? At what age are children able to reliably use motor imagery? These insights are necessary to judge the feasibility of motor imagery training to promote motor performance in young children with congenital motor disorders (Steenbergen et al., 2009.

Title: Motor imagery training improves upper extremity performance in stroke patients
Snippet: [Purpose] The purpose of this study was to investigate whether motor imagery training has a positive influence on upper extremity performance in stroke patients. [Subjects and Methods] Twenty-four patients were randomly assigned to one of the following two groups: motor imagery (n = 12) or control (n = 12). Over the course of 4 weeks, the motor imagery group participated in 30 minutes of motor imagery training on each of the 18 tasks (9 hours total) related to their daily living activities. After the 4-week intervention period, the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity outcomes and Wolf Motor Function Test outcomes were compared. [Results] The post-test score of the motor imagery group on the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity outcomes was significantly higher than that of the control group. In particular, the shoulder and wrist sub-items demonstrated improvement in the motor imagery group. [Conclusion] Motor imagery training has a positive influence on upper extremity performance by improving functional mobility during stroke rehabilitation. These results suggest that motor imagery training is feasible and beneficial for improving upper extremity function in stroke patients.

Title: Influence of motor imagery training on gait rehabilitation in sub-acute stroke: A randomized controlled trial.
Snippet: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the effect of mental practice on motor imagery ability and assess the influence of motor imagery on gait rehabilitation in sub-acute stroke.


DESIGN
Randomized controlled trial.


SUBJECTS
A total of 44 patients with gait dysfunction after first-ever stroke were randomly allocated to a motor imagery training group and a muscle relaxation group.


METHODS
The motor imagery group received 6 weeks of daily mental practice. The relaxation group received a muscle relaxation programme of equal duration. Motor imagery ability and lower limb function were assessed at baseline and after 6 weeks of treatment. Motor imagery ability was tested using a questionnaire and mental chronometry test. Gait outcome was evaluated using a 10-m walk test (near transfer) and the Fugl-Meyer assessment (far transfer).


RESULTS
Significant between-group differences were found, with the vividness of kinesthetic imagery and the walking test results improving more in the motor imagery group than in the muscle relaxation group. There was no group interaction effect for the far transfer outcome score.


CONCLUSION
Motor imagery training may have a beneficial task-specific effect on gait function in sub-acute stroke; however, longer term confirmation is required.

Title: A Single-Session Preliminary Evaluation of an Affordable BCI-Controlled Arm Exoskeleton and Motor-Proprioception Platform
Snippet: To evaluate the performance of the BCI training device, nine stroke participants were recruited. Next, they used the training device to perform goal-directed motor tasks (15-30 min). snippet.text: In a series of studies that have appeared in the last decade (Tamir et al., 2007;Lee et al., 2011;Page et al., 2011;Cho et al., 2012), it was shown that motor imagery training can be beneficial for motor rehabilitation in adult patients with acquired brain damage, in particular stroke (for reviews see Sharma et al., 2006;Dickstein and Deutsch, 2007;Zimmermann-Schlatter et al., 2008;Malouin and Richards, 2010). Motor imagery is supposed to stimulate the neural networks that underlie the planning and control of movements. As such, motor imagery training in rehabilitation is regarded as a 'backdoor' to facilitate a patient's motor performance (Sharma et al., 2006). Despite its proven effectiveness for rehabilitation in adult stroke patients, and despite converging evidence showing that problems in motor imagery are concomitant with motor control problems in congenital motor disorders such as cerebral palsy (CP) and developmental coordination disorder (DCD; Wilson et al., 2001;Crajé et al., 2010), empirical studies on motor imagery training in these children are scarce (but see Wilson et al., 2002). A likely reason for this lack of research may be that the successful application of motor imagery training necessitates that the individual has a skilled capacity to perform motor imagery. While adults were repeatedly shown to be able to use motor imagery (e.g., Cerritelli et al., 2000;Petit et al., 2003;Choudhury et al., 2007a;ter Horst et al., 2012), children's ability for motor imagery is not very clear. The present study reviews the empirical literature on motor imagery in children to delineate the capacity of children up to 12 years of age to engage in motor imagery. The studies that were selected after a search in the literature are analyzed to provide answers to two research questions. How does motor imagery develop during childhood? At what age are children able to reliably use motor imagery? These insights are necessary to judge the feasibility of motor imagery training to promote motor performance in young children with congenital motor disorders (Steenbergen et al., 2009.

OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the effect of mental practice on motor imagery ability and assess the influence of motor imagery on gait rehabilitation in sub-acute stroke.


DESIGN
Randomized controlled trial.


SUBJECTS
A total of 44 patients with gait dysfunction after first-ever stroke were randomly allocated to a motor imagery training group and a muscle relaxation group.


METHODS
The motor imagery group received 6 weeks of daily mental practice. The relaxation group received a muscle relaxation programme of equal duration. Motor imagery ability and lower limb function were assessed at baseline and after 6 weeks of treatment. Motor imagery ability was tested using a questionnaire and mental chronometry test. Gait outcome was evaluated using a 10-m walk test (near transfer) and the Fugl-Meyer assessment (far transfer).


RESULTS
Significant between-group differences were found, with the vividness of kinesthetic imagery and the walking test results improving more in the motor imagery group than in the muscle relaxation group. There was no group interaction effect for the far transfer outcome score.


CONCLUSION
Motor imagery training may have a beneficial task-specific effect on gait function in sub-acute stroke; however, longer term confirmation is required.

To evaluate the performance of the BCI training device, nine stroke participants were recruited. During the training session of the experiment, the participants went through BCI training (30-45 min) and the FES unit set up (10-20 min). Next, they used the training device to perform goal-directed motor tasks (15-30 min). The participants were also assessed for their motor-proprioception ability before and after the training session using a motor-proprioception assessment protocol we developed. Further, we used the upper-extremity subtest of the Fugl-Meyer (FM) test to examine the impairment severity of all stroke participants (Gladstone et al., 2002). We also used kinesthetic and visual imagery questionnaire short version (KVIQ-10) (Malouin et al., 2007) to quantify the motor imagery ability of the participants. 

Nine male stroke participants (mean age 66 ± 11.9 years) agreed to participate in this study. The demographics and preassessment results of the participants are presented in Table 1. One participant (P01) had expressive aphasia [15/30 on the Frenchay Aphasia Assessment (Al-Khawaja et al., 1996)] and was unable to complete the MoCA test. Nevertheless, he was still included in this study to explore if individuals with expressive aphasia could operate the training device. The FM scores of the participants ranged from 11 to 63, suggesting mild to severe motor impairments. All participants were also tested on the KVIQ to assess their imagery ability. All participants scored above 29 out of 50.
